glosses_en: The first letter of the Corsican alphabet, called a and written in the Latin script.

o.etymology: From Latin aut. Cognates include Italian o and Spanish o.

aria.etymology: From Latin aer, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀήρ (aḗr). Cognates include Italian aria and French air.

ci.etymology: Ultimately from either Latin hīc (“here”) or hinc (“from here”). Akin to Italian ci; see there for more. Compare Sicilian cci.

glosses_en: you (plural, both direct or indirect object)
vi.etymology: From voi (“you”). Compare Italian vi and Romanian vi.

glosses_en: USSR (initialism of Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, official name of Soviet Union: a former transcontinental country in Europe and Asia (1922–1991), now split into Russia and 14 other countries)

cane.etymology: From Latin canis, canem (“dog”). Cognates with Italian cane, French chien, Sicilian cani.

zebra.etymology: From Portuguese zebra (“wild horse”), from zebro, from Old Galician-Portuguese zevro, from *ezevro, from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin *equiferus, from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”).

lama.etymology: Borrowed from French lame. Cognates include Italian lama.

glosses_en: second-person singular indicative present of avè
Deuxième personne du singulier du présent de l'indicatif de avè.

so.etymology: From Vulgar Latin sum, from Latin suum, from Proto-Italic *sowos, from Proto-Indo-European *sewos. Cognates include Italian suo and French son.

grazie.etymology: Plural of grazia (“grace”), from Latin gratia, as used in the phrase grātiās agō (“to thank; to express thanks”). Akin to Italian grazie.

sale.etymology: From Latin salem, accusative of sāl.

ride.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin rīdere, from Latin rīdēre.

glosses_en: Africa (the continent south of Europe and between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans)
Africa.etymology: Inherited from Latin Āfrica. Cognate with Italian Africa and French Afrique.

glosses_en: Asia (the largest continent, located between Europe and the Pacific Ocean)
Asia.etymology: From Latin Asia, from Ancient Greek Ἀσία (Asía). Compare Italian Asia and Spanish Asia.

glosses_en: Le, déterminant introduisant un nom masculin singulier.
u.etymology: From the earlier lu. Compare Portuguese o and Aragonese o.

un.etymology: Inherited from Latin ūnus (“one”), from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos. Cognates include Italian un (“a”) and French un (“a, one”).

sei.etymology: From Latin sex, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs. Cognates include Italian sei and Spanish seis.

sette.etymology: From Latin septem, from Proto-Italic *septem, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Cognates include Italian sette and Portuguese sete.

nove.etymology: From Latin novem, from Proto-Italic *nowem, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognates include Italian nove and Portuguese nove.

casa.etymology: From Latin casa. Cognates include Italian casa and Spanish casa.

li.etymology: From Latin illi, masculine plural of ille, from Old Latin olle. Cognates include Italian gli (“the, them”) and Romanian îi (“them”).

thee, you (singular; both direct and indirect object)
ti.etymology: Inherited from Latin te. Cognates include Italian te, ti and French te.

la.etymology: From Latin illa, feminine form of ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle. Cognates include Italian la and French la.

lu.etymology: From Latin ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle (“that”). Cognates include Italian lo (“him”), il (“the”) and French le (“the, him”).

glosses_en: The twenty-second letter of the Corsican alphabet, called esge and written in the Latin script.

noi.etymology: From Latin nos, from Proto-Italic *nōs. Cognates include Italian noi and Romanian noi.

glosses_en: Pronom de la deuxième personne du pluriel : vous.
voi.etymology: From Latin vos, from Old Latin vos, from Proto-Italic *wōs. Cognates include Italian voi and Romanian voi.

sì.etymology: From Latin sīc est (“so it is”). Cognates include Italian sì and Spanish sí.

vacca.etymology: From Latin vacca. Cognates include Italian vacca and Spanish vaca.

serra.etymology: From Latin serra (“saw”), from Proto-Italic *serzā, from Proto-Indo-European *sers- (“to cut off”). Cognates include Portuguese serra and Spanish sierra.

glosses_en: Forms the passive voice; to be
Forms the perfect aspect of some verbs; to have
esse.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin essere, from Inherited from Latin esse. Compare Italian essere, French être.

luna.etymology: From Latin lūna, from Proto-Italic *louksnā, from Proto-Indo-European *lówksneh₂.

manu.etymology: Inherited from Latin manus. Compare Italian mano.

acqua.etymology: Inherited from Latin aqua (“water”). Cognates include Italian acqua and French eau.

elefante.etymology: Borrowed from Latin elephantem, accusative of elephas, from Ancient Greek ἐλέφᾱς (eléphās). Cognates include Italian elefante and Spanish elefante.

apa.etymology: From Latin apis. Cognates include Italian ape and Neapolitan apa.

carta.etymology: From Latin charta, borrowed from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs). Cognates include Italian carta and Spanish carta.

banca.etymology: Of Germanic origin. Akin to Italian banca, see there for more.

stella.etymology: From Latin stella, from Proto-Italic *stērlā, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂stḗr. Cognates include Italian stella and Romanian stea.

glosses_en: China (a cultural region and civilization in East Asia, occupying the region around the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl Rivers, taken as a whole under its various dynasties)
China (a large country in East Asia, occupying the region around the Yellow, Yangtze, and Pearl Rivers; the People's Republic of China, since 1949)
Cina.etymology: Ultimately from Sanskrit चीन (Cīna), from Old Chinese 秦 (*zin). Compare Italian Cina and Portuguese China.

terra.etymology: From Latin terra, from Proto-Italic *terza. Cognates include Gallurese tarra, Italian terra and French terre.

è.etymology: From Latin et, from Proto-Indo-European *éti. Cognates include Italian e and Portuguese e.

le.etymology: From Latin illae, feminine plural of ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle. Cognates include Italian le (“the, them”) and French les (“the, them”).

una.etymology: Inherited from Latin una, feminine of unus. Cognates include Italian una and Spanish una.

aprile.etymology: From Latin Aprīlis. Cognates include Italian aprile and French avril.

là.etymology: From Latin labii, the first word of the sixth line of Ut queant laxis, on which the names for the notes of the solfège were based. Compare Italian la and French la.

spada.etymology: From Latin spatha, from Ancient Greek σπάθη (spáthē). Cognates include Italian spada and Spanish espada.

glosses_en: Sardinia (an island and autonomous region of Italy, in the Mediterranean Sea)

fica.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *fica, from Latin ficus. Cognates include Italian fica (“fig fruit, pussy”) and Occitan figa (“fig”).

assai.etymology: From Late Latin ad satis. Cognates include Sicilian assai, Italian assai and French assez.

core.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *corem m, from Latin cor n.

mille.etymology: From Latin mille, from Proto-Italic *smīɣeslī, from Proto-Indo-European *smih₂ǵʰéslih₂. Cognates include Italian mille and French mille.

hour (a unit of time of one twenty-fourth of a day (sixty minutes))

animale.etymology: From Latin animal. Cognates include Italian animale and French animal.

elle.etymology: From Latin illae, feminine plural form of ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle (“that”). Cognates include Italian elle (“they”) and French elles (“they”).

glosses_en: Spain (a country in Southern Europe, including most of the Iberian peninsula)
England (a constituent country of the United Kingdom)

regione.etymology: Borrowed from Latin regio. Cognates include Italian regione and French région.

anca.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *hanca (“hip”), from Frankish *hanka, from Proto-Germanic *ankijǭ (“joint”), from Proto-Indo-European *ang- (“joint”). Cognates include Italian anca (“hip”) and French hanche (“hip”).

verde.etymology: From Late Latin virdis, syncopated from Latin viridis. Cognates include Italian verde and French vert.

università.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin universitas. Cognates include Italian università and French université.

geografia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin geōgraphia, from Ancient Greek γεωγραφία (geōgraphía).

signora.etymology: From Medieval Latin seniōra. Cognate with Italian signora.

atmosfera.etymology: From French atmosphère, from New Latin atmosphaera, from Ancient Greek ἀτμός (atmós, “steam”) + σφαῖρα (sphaîra, “sphere”). Akin to Italian atmosfera.

traduce.etymology: From Latin traducere, from Proto-Italic *tranzdoukō. Cognates include Italian tradurre and French traduire.

grazia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin grātia (“favour; goodwill; charm”). Cognates include Italian grazia, French grâce, Sicilian grazzia, Spanish gracia.

glosses_en: bun; chignon (roll or twist of hair worn at the nape of the neck)
cipolla.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

medicina.etymology: From Latin medicina. Cognates include Italian medicina and French médecine.

glosses_en: Arabia (a peninsula of West Asia between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf; includes Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, and the United Arab Emirates)
Arabia (the region of West Asia within or adjacent to the Arabian Plate; Yemen, Oman, Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the Egyptian Sinai, Palestine and the United Arab Emirates)
Arabia.etymology: From Latin Arabia, from Ancient Greek Ἀραβία (Arabía).

opossum.etymology: Borrowed from English opossum, from Powhatan aposoum (“white animal”).

glosses_en: Corsica (an island and administrative region of France, in the Mediterranean to the north of Sardinia)
Corsica.etymology: Borrowed from Latin Corsica (from Ancient Greek Κορσίς (Korsís)).

lettu.etymology: From Latin lectus (“bed”). Cognates include Italian letto and French lit.

dui.etymology: From Latin duo, from Proto-Italic *duō, from Proto-Indo-European *dwóh₁. Cognates include Italian due, Romanian doi, Sicilian dui.

unu.etymology: From Latin unus, from Old Latin oinos, from Proto-Italic *oinos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁óynos. Cognates include Italian uno, Romanian unu, Sicilian unu.

bè.etymology: From Latin bene, from Old Latin *duened, from Old Latin duenos. Cognates include Italian bene and French bien.

diu.etymology: From Latin deus, from Old Latin deivos, from Proto-Italic *deiwos, from Proto-Indo-European *deywós. Cognates include Italian dio and French dieu.

luni.etymology: From Latin Lunae diēs. Cognates include Italian lunedì, French lundi, Sicilian luni.

teste.etymology: From English teste, perhaps via or else akin to Italian teste.

risa.etymology: From Latin risa, feminine past participle of rideo. Cognates include Italian riso and Spanish risa.

volpe.etymology: From Latin vulpes, from Proto-Italic *wolpis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wl̥p-i-s (“marten, cat”). Cognates include Italian volpe and Romanian vulpe.

europeu.etymology: From Latin Europaeus. Cognates include Italian europeo and Portuguese europeu.

sud.etymology: Borrowed from French sud. Cognates include Italian sud and Spanish sur.

glosses_en: Pronom masculin de la troisième personne du pluriel : ils, eux.
elli.etymology: From Latin illi, plural of ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle (“that”). Cognates include Italian elli and Romanian ei.

cù.etymology: From Latin cum, from Old Latin com, from Proto-Italic *kom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm (“next to, along”). Cognates include Italian con and Romanian cu.

lupu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *lūpum, from Latin lŭpum. Compare Italian lupo.

arba.etymology: From Latin herba. Cognates include Italian erba and French herbe.

glosses_en: Netherlands (the main constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, located primarily in Western Europe bordering Germany and Belgium)
Netherlands (a country in Western Europe, consisting of four constituent countries: the Netherlands per se, Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten the Kingdom of the Netherlands)

sega.etymology: From the verb segà (“to saw”). Akin to Italian sega and French scie.

annu.etymology: From Latin annus, from Proto-Italic *atnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂et-no-. Cognates include Italian anno and Portuguese ano.

ossu.etymology: From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst.

issu.etymology: Probably from Latin ipse (“himself”). Cognates include Italian esso (“it”), Portuguese isso (“this, that”) and Sicilian ssu.

isula.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *isula, from Latin īnsula.

mula.etymology: From Latin mula, feminine of mulus.

marti.etymology: From Latin Mārtis diēs. Cognates include Italian martedì and French mardi.

brocciu.etymology: From a pre-Roman word whence also Catalan brossa (“litter; brushwood”) and Occitan brossa (“brushwood”).

mele.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *melem m or f, from Latin mel n.

negligenza.etymology: Borrowed from Latin negligentia. Cognates include Italian negligenza and French négligence.

settembre.etymology: From Latin September. Compare Italian settembre.

ottobre.etymology: From Latin Octōber. Compare Italian ottobre.

dicembre.etymology: From Latin December. Compare Italian dicembre.

misericordia.etymology: From Latin misericordia. Cognates include Italian misericordia and Spanish misericordia.

sumere.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *saumarius, alternative form of Late Latin sagmarius (“having a saddle”). Cognates include Italian somaro (“donkey”) and Old French somier (“bag”).

geologia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin geōlogia, from Ancient Greek γεω- (geō-) + Latin -logia, from Ancient Greek -λογία (-logía).

talianu.etymology: From Latin italianus. Compare Sicilian talianu and Italian italiano.

grecu.etymology: From Latin Graecus, from Ancient Greek Γραικός (Graikós).

cità.etymology: From Latin civitas. Cognates include Italian città and French cité.

vinti.etymology: From Latin viginti, from Proto-Italic *wīgentī, from Proto-Indo-European *dwi(h₁)dḱm̥ti. Cognates include Italian venti and Portuguese vinte.

radio-.etymology: Ultimately from French radio-. Akin to Italian radio- and Spanish radio-.

chè.etymology: From Latin quid (“what”), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid. Cognates include Italian che (“what, that”) and French que (“what, that”).

chì.etymology: From Latin quis, from Proto-Italic *kʷis, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷís. Cognates include Italian chi and French qui.

què.etymology: Ultimately from Latin eccum (perhaps via some compound), from ecce + eum.

tù.etymology: From Latin tu, from Proto-Italic *tū, from Proto-Indo-European *túh₂. Cognates include Italian tu and French tu.

foglia.etymology: From Late Latin folia, from the plural of Latin folium (“leaf”), probably from Proto-Indo-European *bʰolh₃yom (“leaf”), from *bʰleh₃- (“blossom, flower”).

ella.etymology: From Latin illa, feminine form of ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle (“that”). Cognates include Italian ella and Spanish ella.

United States (a country in North America)

odore.etymology: From Latin odōrem, from an archaic form odōs, from Proto-Italic *odōs, from Proto-Indo-European *h₃édos, derived from the root *h₃ed- (“to smell, stink”).

prete.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *previter, from Latin presbyter (“elder”), from Ancient Greek πρεσβύτερος (presbúteros, “elder”). Cognates include Italian prete and French prêtre.

solu.etymology: From Latin sōlus. Cognate with Italian solo.

nucleare.etymology: From nucleu (“nucleus”) + -are. Akin to Italian nucleare and French nucléaire.

visone.etymology: Borrowed from French vison, from Old French vison. Cognates include Italian visone and Spanish visón.

amà.etymology: From Latin amāre. Compare Italian amare.

rettile.etymology: From Late Latin reptile, from Latin reptilis (“crawling”). Cognates include Italian rettile and French reptile.

biochimica.etymology: From bio- + chimica (“chemistry”). Akin to Italian biochimica.

pece.etymology: From Latin pix, picem, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *pī́ts (“pitch; resin”). Cognates include Italian pece and English pitch.

tuttu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin tottus, alteration of Classical Latin totus. Cognates include Italian tutto, Sicilian tuttu and Portuguese tudo.

zeru.etymology: From Medieval Latin zephirum, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr). Cognates include Italian zero and French zéro.

mè.etymology: From Latin me. Cognates include Italian me and French moi.

lucente.etymology: From Latin lucens. Compare Italian lucente.

lontra.etymology: From a Vulgar Latin variant of Latin lutra. Cognates include Italian lontra, French loutre.

figliu.etymology: From Latin filius. Cognate to Italian figlio.

istu.etymology: From Latin iste (“that”). Cognates include Italian esto (“this”) and Spanish este (“this”).

Kazakistan.etymology: Borrowed from another Romance language, ultimately from Russian Казахстан (Kazaxstan). Compare Italian Kazakistan, Spanish Kazajistán and Portuguese Cazaquistão.

tassu.etymology: From Late Latin taxus, borrowed from Proto-Germanic *þahsuz. Cognates include Italian tasso and Galician teixo.

bonu.etymology: From Latin bonus, from Old Latin duonus, from Proto-Italic *dwenos. Cognates include Italian buono and French bon.

albu.etymology: From Latin albus, from Proto-Italic *alβos, from Proto-Indo-European *albʰós. Cognates include Italian albo and Portuguese alvo.

cantà.etymology: From Latin cantāre. Compare Gallurese cantà and Italian cantare.

ottu.etymology: From Latin octō, from Proto-Italic *oktō, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Cognates include Italian otto and Portuguese oito.

quattru.etymology: From Latin quattuor, from Proto-Italic *kʷettwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwóres. Cognates include Italian quattro and Portuguese quatro.

trè.etymology: From Latin tres, from Proto-Italic *trēs, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Cognates include Italian tre and Romanian trei.

parlà.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin parabolare. Cf. Italian parlare.

tondu.etymology: Clipping of rutondu. Akin to Italian tondo.

beddu.etymology: From Latin bellus, a diminutive of bonus (“good”). Cognate with Italian bello, Sicilian beḍḍu.

marsupiale.etymology: From French marsupial, from Latin marsupium (“pouch”), from Ancient Greek μάρσιππος (mársippos).

neru.etymology: From older negru, from Latin nigrum. Cf. Italian nero, negro.

canzona.etymology: From Latin cantio. Cognates include Gallurese canzona, Italian canzone and French chanson.

centu.etymology: From Latin centum, from Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm.

domu.etymology: From Latin domus, from Proto-Italic *domos, from Proto-Indo-European *dṓm. Cognates include Sicilian domu and Sardinian domu.

esegesi.etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “I explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “I lead, guide”).

sudeste.etymology: From sud (“south”) + este (“east”). Compare French sud-est and Italian sudest.

seculu.etymology: Probably a semi-learned borrowing from Latin sēculum (“lifetime, age”), from saeculum (“lifetime, age”). Compare Italian secolo, Sicilian sèculu.

focu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin focus, of uncertain origin. Cognates include Italian fuoco and French feu.

etimulugia.etymology: From Latin etymologia, from Ancient Greek ἐτυμολογία (etumología, “etymology”).

glosses_en: Leiden (a city in South Holland, Netherlands)

ugna.etymology: Ultimately from Latin ungula (< unguis), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-. Cognate with Italian unghia, Sicilian ugna.

rossu.etymology: From Latin russus, from Proto-Italic *roussos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ-. Cognates include Italian rosso and French rouge.

furmicula.etymology: From Late Latin formicula, from Latin formica, from Proto-Indo-European *morwi-. Compare Sicilian furmìcula and Italian formicola.

capu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin capus, masculinization of Latin caput.

granu.etymology: From Latin granum. Cognate with Sicilian granu.

iè.etymology: From Late Latin illī est (“it is”).

ghjinochju.etymology: From Late Latin genuculum, alteration of Latin geniculum, diminutive of genū (“knee”). Cognates include Gallurese ghinocchiu, Italian ginocchio and French genou.

intinghje.etymology: From Late Latin intingere, from Latin tingō.

manzu.etymology: Possibly from Illyrian. Compare Italian manzo.

statu.etymology: From Latin status. Cognates include Gallurese statu, Italian stato and Romanian stat.

biera.etymology: Ultimately from Frankish *beuʀ, from Proto-Germanic *beuzą. Compare French bière and Italian birra.

cantu.etymology: From Latin cantus. Cognates include Gallurese cantu, Italian canto and French chant.

segà.etymology: From Latin secare (“to cut”), from Proto-Indo-European *sek-. Cognates include Italian segare and Spanish segar.

glosses_en: (précédé de ci) Falloir. Note d’usage : Le son v de la racine disparaît optionnellement, donnant ci vole \'t͡ʃo.le\, ci vulia \t͡ʃu.'li.a\ etc.
vulè.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin volēre, from Latin velle.

questu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum iste, from Latin eccum (“there he is”) + iste (“this”). Compare Italian questo and Spanish aqueste.

mercuri.etymology: From Latin dies Mercurii. Cognates include Romanian miercuri, Italian mercoledì and Spanish miércoles.

dece.etymology: From Latin decem, from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥. Cognates include Italian diece, dieci and Portuguese dez.

caminu.etymology: From Latin camīnus, from Ancient Greek κάμῑνος (kámīnos). Cognates include Italian camino, French cheminée and English chimney (via Old French).

teatru.etymology: From Latin theātrum, from Ancient Greek θέᾱτρον (théātron, “a place for viewing”).

banchieru.etymology: From banca (“bank”) + -ieru. Compare Italian banchiere and French banquier.

buttiglia.etymology: From Old French boteille. Compare French bouteille and Portuguese botelha.

bichjeru.etymology: From Late Latin bicarium. Cognates include Italian bicchiere and French pichet (“jug”).

butiru.etymology: From Latin butyrum, from Ancient Greek βούτυρον (boúturon). Cognates include Italian burro and Spanish butiro.

millanta.etymology: From mille (“thousand”) + -anta. Akin to Italian millanta.

mulu.etymology: From Latin mulus. Cognates include Italian mulo and Portuguese mulo.

sapè.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *sapēre, from Classical Latin sapere (“taste, know”).

glosses_en: chief town or city of a region; capital city.

chjamà.etymology: From Latin clamare. Cognates include Italian chiamare and French clamer.

vechju.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin veclus, from Latin vetulus. Compare Italian vecchio.

glosses_en: June (the sixth month of the year on the Gregorian calendar.)

lugliu.etymology: From Latin iūlius, through a process of dissimilation, as with Italian luglio.

aostu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin agustus, from Latin augustus. Cognates include Italian agosto and French août.

nuvembre.etymology: From Latin November. Compare Italian novembre.

ghjennaghju.etymology: From Vulgar Latin ienuārius, from Latin Iānuārius.

ferraghju.etymology: From Late Latin Febrārius, from Latin Februārius.

maghju.etymology: From Latin Maius. Compare Italian maggio.

manghjà.etymology: From Late Latin manducare. Cognates include Italian mangiare and French manger.

cumprà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *comperāre, from Latin comparāre (“prepare, procure, get, purchase, obtain”).

sittimana.etymology: From Late Latin septimāna (“week”), from the Latin septimānus (“related to the seventh element of a series”, adjective), derived from septimus (“seventh”).

ghjovi.etymology: From Latin Jovis diēs or Iovis diēs, variant of diēs Iovis (“day of Jupiter”). Compare Italian giovedì.

vennari.etymology: From Latin Veneris diēs, variant of diēs Veneris (“day of Venus”). Compare Italian venerdì and French vendredi.

dumenica.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin [diēs] Dominica (literally “day of the Lord”). Compare Italian domenica, French dimanche, Sicilian dumìnica.

cunnosce.etymology: From Late Latin conōscere, variant of Latin cognōscere.

abbaghjà.etymology: Of onomatopoeic origin. Compare French aboyer and Italian abbaiare.

accumpagnà.etymology: From a- + cumpagnu (“companion”) + -à. Compare Italian accompagnare and French accompagner.

aiutà.etymology: From Latin adiūtāre. Cognates include Italian aiutare and Romanian ajuta.

alzà.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *altiāre, derived from Latin altus (“high”). Compare Italian alzare.

andà.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin andāre, of uncertain origin.

appruntà.etymology: From a- + prontu (“ready”) + -à. Compare Italian approntare.

ghjucà.etymology: Inherited from Latin iocārī. Compare Italian giocare.

sangui.etymology: From Vulgar Latin sanguem, alteration of Latin sanguinem, accusative of sanguis.

stonda.etymology: From Germanic, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *stundō (“period of time”), possibly through Catalan estona.

porcu.etymology: From Latin porcus, from Proto-Italic *porkos, from Proto-Indo-European *pórḱos. Cognates include Italian porco, Portuguese porco and Sicilian porcu.

zebru.etymology: From Portuguese zebro (“wild horse”), from Old Galician-Portuguese zevro, from earlier *ezevro, from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus, from equus (“horse”) + ferus (“wild”).

bellula.etymology: From bella (“handsome”) + -ula. Calque of French belette by reanalysing it as a diminutive of belle (“handsome”).

nudu.etymology: From Latin nudus, from Proto-Italic *nogʷedos, from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷ-.

fraula.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *frāgula, diminutive of Latin frāga, plural of frāgum. Cf. Italian fragola.

camellu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *camellus, from Latin camelus, from Ancient Greek κάμηλος (kámēlos), from a Semitic language. Cognates include Italian cammello and Portuguese camelo.

abetu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *abētem, from Classical Latin abietem.

gallu.etymology:
Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *gelH-der.?
Latin gallus
Corsican gallu
Inherited from Latin gallus, possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gelH-.

Diu.etymology: From Latin Deus, from deus. See further etymology on diu. Cognates include Italian Dio and French Dieu.

glosses_en: a male given name from Ancient Greek, equivalent to English Peter
Petru.etymology: Ultimately from Ancient Greek Πετρος (Petros), from πέτρος (pétros, “stone, rock”), related to πέτρα (pétra).

levra.etymology: From Latin lepus. Cognates include Italian lepre and French lièvre.

glosses_en: Belgium (a country in Western Europe that has borders with the Netherlands, Germany, Luxembourg and France)
Belgica.etymology: From Latin Belgica. Cognates include French Belgique and Spanish Bélgica.

acula.etymology: From Latin aquila. Cognates include Italian aquila and French aigle.

glosses_en: The fourth letter of the Corsican alphabet, called chjì and written in the Latin script.
The ninth letter of the Corsican alphabet, called ghjè and written in the Latin script.
Forms the perfect aspect; to have
avè.etymology: From Latin habēre, from Proto-Italic *habēō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰeh₁bʰ- (“to grab”). Cognates include Italian avere and Romanian avea.

boscu.etymology: Inherited from Early Medieval Latin boscus, borrowed from Frankish *busk, from Proto-Germanic *buskaz.

corsu.etymology: From Latin Corsus. Cognates include Italian corso and Portuguese corso, Asturian and Sicilian corsu.

Proto-Italic *orsos

Inherited from Latin ursus, from Proto-Italic *orsos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ŕ̥tḱos.

biancu.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin blancus. Compare Italian bianco and Gallurese biancu.

quindeci.etymology: From Latin quindecim. Cognates include Italian quindici and Spanish quince.

nordu.etymology: Borrowed from French nord. Cognates include Italian nord and Spanish norte.

mansu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *mānsus, from Latin mansuetus.

glosses_en: A unit of measure equal to four hands (about 16 inches).
bracciu.etymology: From Latin bracchium, from Ancient Greek βραχίων (brakhíōn). Cognates include Italian braccio and Portuguese braço.

glosses_en: body (the physical structure of a human or animal)
body (any physical object or material thing)
corps, body, organization (group of people with a common purpose)
corpu.etymology: Inherited from Latin corpus, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱrep-.

ghjacaru.etymology:
Probably from Vulgar Latin *cattulus (“whelp, puppy”), from Latin catŭlus (“puppy”).
Or, from or influenced by a metathesis of Basque txakur, xakur (“puppy”); however, this has been dismissed as speculative. Compare Spanish cachorro and Sar

glosses_en: The name of the Latin script letter Ghj/ghj.
The name of the Latin script letter Chj/chj.
The fourth letter of the Corsican alphabet, written in the Latin script.
The ninth letter of the Corsican alphabet, written in the Latin script.

novu.etymology: From Latin novus from Proto-Italic *nowos, from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, from the root *new-.

azotu.etymology: Borrowed from French azote. Compare Italian azoto.

ghjattu.etymology: From Latin cattus. Cognates include Italian gatto and Spanish gato.

amicu.etymology: From Latin amicus. Cognates include Italian amico and Portuguese amigo.

argentu.etymology: From Latin argentum, from Proto-Italic *argentom. Cognates include Italian argento and French argent.

giallu.etymology: Borrowed from Old French jalne, from Latin galbinus. Cognates include Italian giallo and French jaune.

Genoa (a port city and comune, the capital of the Metropolitan City of Genoa and the region of Liguria, Italy)
Genoa (a metropolitan city of Liguria, established in 2015; in full, the Metropolitan City of Genoa)
Paris (the capital and largest city of France)

eiu.etymology: Inherited from Late Latin eo, from Classical Latin egō̆. Compare Italian io and Sicilian ju,

ellu.etymology: From Latin ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle (“that”). Cognates include Italian egli (“he”), French il (“he”), Sicilian iḍḍu.

quellu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum ille, from eccum (“behold him”) + ille (“that”), from Old Latin olle. Cognates include Italian quello (“that”) and Spanish aquel (“that”).

quissu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *eccum ipse, from eccum (“behold”) + ipse (“the very same”). Cognate with Sicilian chissu.

glosses_en: Ce, ce ... -là (neutre ou à proximité de l'écouteur).

ondeci.etymology: From Latin undecim. Cognates include Italian undici and French onze.

dodeci.etymology: From Latin duodecim. Cognates include Sicilian dùdici, Italian dodici and Spanish doce.

tredeci.etymology: From Latin trēdecim. Cognates include Italian tredici and Spanish trece.

quattordeci.etymology: From Latin quattuordecim. Cognates include Italian quattordici and Spanish catorce.

sedeci.etymology: From Latin sēdecim. Cognates include Italian sedici and French seize.

dicessette.etymology: From dece (“ten”) + sette (“seven”). Akin to French dix-sept and Italian diciassette.

diciottu.etymology: From dece (“ten”) + ottu (“eight”). Akin to French dix-huit and Italian diciotto.

dicennove.etymology: From dece (“ten”) + nove (“nine”). Akin to French dix-neuf and Italian diciannove.

migliu.etymology: Ultimately from Latin mille, shortening of an earlier mille passus. Compare Italian miglio, Sicilian migghiu and Spanish milla.

mammiferu.etymology: Akin to Italian mammifero and French mammifère.

acellu.etymology: From Late Latin aucellus m (“little bird”), a diminutive ultimately based on Latin avis f (“bird”), from Proto-Italic *awis, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂éwis. Cognates include Italian uccello and French oiseau.

anfibiu.etymology: From Latin amphibius, from Ancient Greek ἀμφίβιος (amphíbios). Cognates include Italian anfibio and Spanish anfibio.

pesciu.etymology: Inherited from Latin pisce(m) (with a change in the final vowel), from Proto-Indo-European *peysk-. Cognates include Portuguese peixe and Italian pesce.

argentinu.etymology: From Argentina + -u. Compare Italian argentino and Spanish argentino.

cavallu.etymology: From Late Latin caballus, from Latin caballus (“pack horse”), from Gaulish *kaballos, from Proto-Celtic *kaballos. Cognates include Italian cavallo, Portuguese cavalo, Sardinian cabaddu, Sicilian cavaḍḍu.

pesciu grondula.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) and a term probably derived from French grondin (“gurnard”).

pesciu ruvettu.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) and a term, probably derived from its scientific name Ruvettus.

scarmu.etymology: From Latin scalmus, from Ancient Greek σκαλμός (skalmós).

pesciu sega.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) + sega (“saw”). Akin to Italian pesce sega.

disegnu.etymology: From the verb disegnà. Akin to Italian disegno.

stranieru.etymology: From Latin extraneus. Cognates include Italian straniero and Spanish extranjero.

glosses_en: European sea sturgeon, Baltic sturgeon (Acipenser sturio)
pesciu sturiu.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) and a second part, derived from Medieval Latin sturio (“sturgeon”).

rutondu.etymology: From Latin rotundus. Cognates include Italian rotondo and Romanian rotund.

ritondu.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin retundus, from Latin rotundus. Cognates include Italian ritondo and Romanian rătund.

vacca maculata.etymology: From vacca (“peacock blenny”) + maculata, feminine of maculatu (“spotted”).

vacca bianca.etymology: From vacca (“peacock blenny”) + bianca, feminine of biancu.

vacca pregna.etymology: From vacca (“peacock blenny”) + pregna, feminine of pregnu (“pregnant”).

pregnu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *praegnus, from Latin praegnans. Cognates include Italian pregno and Portuguese prenhe.

bavosu.etymology: From bava + -osu. Akin to Italian bavoso.

vacca bavosa.etymology: From vacca (“peacock blenny”) + bavosa, feminine of bavosu (“drooling”).

Dalaï Lama.etymology: Borrowed from Tibetan ཏཱ་ལའི་བླ་མ (tā la'i bla ma), probably indirect. Compare French dalaï-lama or Portuguese dalai lama.

pesciu elefante.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) + elefante (“elephant”), referring to the basking shark's size.

diavule.etymology: From Latin diabolus, from Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos). Cognates include Italian diavolo and Spanish diablo.

anghjulu.etymology: From Latin angelus, from Ancient Greek ἄγγελος (ángelos). Cognates include Italian angelo and French ange.

arabu.etymology: From Arabia + -u. Compare Italian arabo and French arabe.

martellu.etymology: From Late Latin martellus, from Latin marculus, diminutive of marcus. Cognates include Italian martello and Portuguese martelo.

cappellu.etymology: From Early Medieval Latin cappellus, from Late Latin cappa. Compare Italian cappello.

pesciu gendarme.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) + gendarme (“gendarme”), due to the fish's head resembling a bicorne, associated with gendarmes.

pesciu volpe.etymology: From pesciu (“fish”) + volpe (“fox”), the second part probably calqued from the Latin name.

glosses_en: Any shark of the genus Carcharhinus.

grisgiu.etymology: Borrowed from another Romance language, from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz. Cognates include Italian grigio, French gris, Sicilian grisu.

furmiculaiu.etymology: From furmicula (“ant”) + -aiu. Compare French fourmilier and Italian formichiere.

insettu.etymology: Borrowed from Latin insectus (“uncut”). Cognates include Italian insetto and Portuguese inseto.

artropodu.etymology: Ultimately from Ancient Greek ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”) + πούς (poús, “foot”). Compare Italian artropode and Portuguese artrópode.

curdatu.etymology: Compare Portuguese cordado and Italian cordato.

vermu.etymology: From Latin vermis, from Proto-Indo-European *wr̥mis. Cognates include Italian verme and Portuguese verme.

molluscu.etymology: Ultimately from Latin molluscus (“soft-shelled”). Cognates include French mollusque and Italian mollusco.

carnivuru.etymology: Borrowed from Latin carnivorus. Cognates include French carnivore and Italian carnivoro.

zoolugia.etymology: Compare Italian zoologia and French zoologie.

ictiolugia.etymology: Compare Italian ittiologia and French ichtyologie.

cumpagnu.etymology: From Late Latin compāniō, a calque of Proto-West Germanic *gahlaibō, from Proto-Germanic *gahlaibô. Cognates include Italian compagno and French copain.

ambacu.etymology: From Latin ambages. Compare French ambage, ambages and Spanish ambages.

prontu.etymology: From Latin promptus (“readiness”). Cognates include Italian pronto and French prompt.

beccazza.etymology: From beccu + -azza. Compare Italian beccaccia and French bécasse.

caghju.etymology: From Latin coagulum. Doublet of caghja (“snot”) Cognates include Italian caglio and Portuguese coalho.

caghja.etymology: From Latin coagulum (“thickening”). Doublet of caghju (“rennet”).

staghjone.etymology: From Latin statiōnem, accusative of statiō (“outpost”).

parechju.etymology: From Late Latin pariculus, diminutive of Latin pār. Compare Italian parecchio, French pareil.

articulu.etymology: From Latin articulus. Cognates include Italian articolo and French article.

vucale.etymology: From Latin vocalis, short for littera vocalis (“sounding letter”). Cognates include Italian vocale and Portuguese vogal.

cunsunante.etymology: From Latin consonans, short for littera consonans (“resounding letter”). Cognates include Italian consonante and English consonant.

anatumia.etymology: From Latin anatomia. Cognates include Italian anatomia and French anatomie.

ecolugia.etymology: From eco- + -lugia. Akin to Italian ecologia.

embriolugia.etymology: From embrio- + -lugia. Akin to Italian embriologia.

oncolugia.etymology: From onco- + -lugia. Akin to Italian oncologia.

fisiolugia.etymology: From fisio- + -lugia. Akin to Italian fisiologia.

idrogenu.etymology: From French hydrogène. Cognates include Italian idrogeno and Spanish hidrógeno.

eliu.etymology: From English helium, from New Latin helium, from Ancient Greek ἥλιος (hḗlios, “sun”). Cognates include Italian elio and French hélium.

dumà.etymology: From Latin domō, from Proto-Italic *domaō, from Proto-Indo-European *demh₂-. Cognates include Italian domare and Portuguese domar.

foranu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *forānus, from Latin foras. Akin to English foreign.

bellu.etymology:
Inherited from Latin bellus. Cognates include Italian bello, French beau, Sicilian beḍḍu (cf. also
bellu).

glucosiu.etymology: From French glucose, from Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos, “sweetness”). Akin to Italian glucosio.

lattosiu.etymology: From Italian lattosio, from Latin lac.

ornitorincu.etymology: From New Latin ornīthorhynchus, from Ancient Greek ὄρνῑς (órnīs) + ῥύγχος (rhúnkhos). Cognates include Italian ornitorinco and French ornithorynque.

oviparu.etymology: From Latin oviparus. Cognates include Italian oviparo and French ovipare.

sciaccallu.etymology: Borrowed from French chacal, from Turkish çakal, from Ottoman Turkish چقال, from Persian شغال, from Middle Persian 𐬱𐬖𐬀𐬮 (šγal), from Sanskrit सृगाल (sṛgāla), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *ćárguš. Cognates include Italian sciacallo.

lamantinu.etymology: Borrowed from French lamantin, from Spanish manatí. Cognates include Italian lamantino and Romanian lamantin.

glosses_en: San Marino (a landlocked microstate in Southern Europe, located within the borders of Italy)
San Marino (the capital city of San Marino)

cunigliu.etymology: Ultimately from Latin cunīculus. Compare Italian coniglio.

luntanu.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *longitānus, from Latin longe. Cognates include Italian lontano and French lointain.

fruntiera.etymology: From Old Occitan frontiera. Cognates include Italian frontiera and French frontière.

anticu.etymology: From Latin antiquus. Cognates include Italian antico and French antique.

ermellinu.etymology: Ultimately from a West Germanic language (compare Dutch hermelijn, German Hermelin), from Proto-Germanic *harmô. Cognates include Italian ermellino and Romanian hermelină.

brunu.etymology: From Medieval Latin brūnus, from Frankish *brūn, from Proto-Germanic *brūnaz, from Proto-Indo-European *bher-. Cognates include Italian bruno and French brun.

orsu brunu.etymology: From orsu (“bear”) + brunu (“brown”). Akin to Italian orso bruno and French ours brun.

orsu biancu.etymology: From orsu (“bear”) + biancu (“white”). Akin to Italian orso bianco and French ours blanc.

orsu grisgiu.etymology: From orsu (“bear”) + grisgiu (“grey”). Akin to Italian orso grigio.

castoru.etymology: From Latin castor, from Ancient Greek κάστωρ (kástōr), from Doric Greek κάστον (káston, “wood”). Cognates include Italian castoro and French castor.

cricetu.etymology: From Czech křeček. Akin to Italian criceto.

vindetta.etymology: From Latin vindicta. Cognates include Italian vendetta and Sicilian vinnitta.

bonghjornu.etymology: From bonu (“good”) + ghjornu (“day”). Akin to Italian buongiorno and French bonjour.

avvedeci.etymology: Related to Italian arrivederci and French au revoir.

vicinu.etymology: From Late Latin vēcīnus, from Latin vīcīnus. Compare Italian vicino.

third-person singular indicative imperfect of traduce

terrenu.etymology: From Latin terrenus. Cognates include Italian terreno and French terrain.

radioattivu.etymology: Ultimately from French radioactif. By surface analysis, radio- (“radio-”) + attivu (“active”). Akin to Italian radioattivo and Spanish radioactivo.

attivu.etymology: From Latin activus. Cognates include Italian attivo and French actif.

infettà.etymology: From Latin infectare. Cognates include Italian infettare and Spanish infectar.

scientificu.etymology: From Latin scientificus. Cognates include Italian scientifico and French scientifique.

rubru.etymology: From Latin rubrus, from Proto-Italic *ruðros, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rudʰrós. Cognates include Italian rubro.

azuru.etymology: Borrowed from Medieval Latin azzurum, from earlier lazulum, borrowed from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward), from Persian لاجورد. Cognates include Italian azzurro and French azur.

celestu.etymology: From Latin caelestis. Cognates include Italian celeste and French céleste.

glosses_en: Ajaccio (the capital and largest city of Corsica, France)
Aiacciu.etymology: From Latin Adiacium. Compare cognate Old Italian Addiazzo and Sicilian Agghiazzu.

alberu.etymology: From Latin arborem f. For the evolution, see Italian albero.

scornu.etymology: Compare Old French corn (“corner, secluded place”).

carrughju.etymology: From Ligurian caróggio, from Vulgar Latin *quadruvium, for Classical Latin quadrivium (“crossroads”), from quattuor (“four”) + via (“road”). Compare Italian carruggio and Sicilian carruggiu.

glosses_en: to jump, bustle, stir (move with agitation)

unghja.etymology: From Vulgar Latin *ungla < Latin ungula (< unguis), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃nogʰ-. Cognate with Italian unghia, Sicilian ugna.

romiccia.etymology: From Latin rumex, perhaps via Vulgar Latin [Term?].

glosses_en: generic name for plants commonly found in a macchia
machja.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *macla, from Latin macula.

astronumia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin astronomia, from Ancient Greek ἀστρονομία (astronomía), from ἄστρον (ástron) + νόμος (nómos).

biolugia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin biologia, from Ancient Greek βίος (bíos) + -λογία (-logía).

archeolugia.etymology: From Ancient Greek ἀρχαιολογία (arkhaiología), from ἀρχαῖος (arkhaîos) + -λογία (-logía).

antropolugia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin anthrōpologia, from Ancient Greek ἄνθρωπος (ánthrōpos) + -λογία (-logía).

filosufia.etymology: Borrowed from Latin philosophia, from Ancient Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophía), from φίλος (phílos, “beloved”) + σοφία (sophía, “wisdom”).

esegesa.etymology: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐξήγησις (exḗgēsis, “interpretation”), from ἐξηγέομαι (exēgéomai, “I explain, interpret”), from ἐξ (ex, “out”) + ἡγέομαι (hēgéomai, “I lead, guide”).

sonniu.etymology: From Latin somnium (“dream”), derived from somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Italic *swepnos, ultimately from the Proto-Indo-European *swépnos.

nidu.etymology: From Latin nīdus, from Proto-Italic *nizdos (“nest”), from Proto-Indo-European *nisdós (“nest”).

cumeta.etymology: Learned borrowing from Latin comēta, from Ancient Greek κομήτης (komḗtēs, “long-haired”).

fecatu.etymology: From Late Latin fīcātum (“liver”), from Latin iecur fīcātum (“fig-stuffed liver, foie gras”).

i/languages A to L.etymology: From the earlier li. Compare Italian i (“the”) and Romanian îi (“them”).
